purpose: Hydrocortisone is used to reduce swelling, redness, itching, and irritation caused by many conditions such as allergies, skin problems, inflammation, and some hormonal disorders. It can also be used to replace a hormone your body is not making enough of on its own, such as in conditions like Addison's disease. It comes in many forms including creams, pills, and injections depending on what it is being used for.
how_it_works: Hydrocortisone works by mimicking a natural hormone your body already makes called cortisol. It helps calm down your immune system and reduce inflammation, which is what causes symptoms like swelling, redness, and pain. Think of it as turning down the volume on your body's overactive alarm system so you feel better.
common_side_effects: For skin creams: mild burning, stinging, or itching where applied, thinning of the skin with long-term use. For pills or injections: increased appetite, weight gain, trouble sleeping, mood changes, upset stomach, increased blood sugar, and fluid retention (puffy ankles or hands).
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly if you have been on it for a long time — your doctor will need to slowly lower your dose to avoid withdrawal effects. Long-term use can weaken your bones, raise your blood sugar, and increase your risk of infections since it lowers your immune system. Tell your doctor if you have diabetes, osteoporosis, high blood pressure, or any active infections before using this medication. Avoid contact with anyone who has chickenpox or measles while taking this medicine.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on the form and condition being treated. Skin creams are usually applied 1 to 4 times a day to the affected area in a thin layer. Oral tablets for hormone replacement are often taken 1 to 3 times daily, commonly 20 to 30 mg per day total, usually with food to protect your stomach. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's specific instructions for your situation.
